food.text: By around 1870, palm oil had become the primary export of some West African countries. European merchants trading with the region also purchased the oil to use as a cooking fat back in Europe.

In the 19th century, kola nuts were a major commodity of intra-African trade, carried by large caravans from the Asante Empire to markets such as Kano in the Sokoto Caliphate. Their main buyers there were aristocrats and scholars, and the trade also extended to markets in Bornu.

In 1851, the German scholar Heinrich Barth described Kano's huge market as a labyrinth of narrow alleys where everything was sold, from vegetables to slaves. He estimated that at least 50% of Kano's people were enslaved, most of them living in slave villages, and called Kano the greatest emporium of central Africa. Its commerce and manufacturing were abundant behind its 10-mile long clay walls, and it remained one of the last major slave societies, with a high enslaved population long after the Atlantic slave trade had been cut off.

By the 19th century, the coastal Balanta people of Portuguese Guinea, who lived outside Portuguese control, had developed a sophisticated system of growing paddy-rice in reclaimed coastal swamps. Much of this rice was exported to surrounding territories, especially after indigenous rice varieties were replaced by imported ones. The Balanta also took part in the slave trade in this period.

Millet couscous remained one of the main staple foods of Senegambia in West Africa until at least the 19th century. In the wider Sahel region, couscous made from pearl millet or sorghum was a popular traditional staple, often prepared with okra or baobab leaves to improve digestibility and texture.

By around 1870, palm oil was the primary export of some West African countries, and the trade often accompanied oppressive labor practices, as highlighted in the account of Abina Mansah's life. Human rights groups argue that such practices in the palm oil industry continue today. In the 1880s cocoa overtook palm oil with the introduction of colonial European cocoa plantations.

From 1913 to 1914, the peanut business was expanding in Kano and groundnut pyramids were becoming more prominent in the city. In the same years Kano suffered a major drought, which caused a famine. Famines also broke out in the region in 1908, 1920, 1927, 1943, 1951, 1956 and 1958.

Peanut exports from Portuguese Guinea began in the mid-19th century, another crop developed during this period. Peasants in Portuguese-controlled areas grew peanuts mixed with food crops and kept fallow periods, since intensive plantation cultivation had already reduced soil fertility elsewhere.

Palm oil, pressed from the fruit of the African oil palm, was used as a cooking ingredient in West African dishes such as egusi soup and okra soup. Its highly saturated fat kept it solid at room temperature in temperate regions, making it a cheap substitute for butter.

Kola nuts were used as an ingredient in Coca-Cola when it launched in 1886, and in Pepsi-Cola when it launched in 1893. This built on their earlier role as a major commodity of 19th-century intra-African trade.

art.text: African wax prints, also called Dutch wax prints or Ankara, became a common material for clothing in West Africa. Dutch merchants introduced them during the 19th century, taking inspiration from native Indonesian batik designs. They adapted the designs and colours to suit the tastes of the African market.

The Great Mosque of Djenné was established in the 14th century but demolished in the early 19th century. It was rebuilt in 1906 to 1907 under the direction of Ismaila Traoré, with guidance from French engineers. It is now the largest earthen building in sub-Saharan Africa.

On February 18, 1897, British forces arrived in Benin City to take reprisals for the loss of trade representatives in a skirmish. Another passage in the article describes it as retaliation for the murder of British diplomats. The Oba's compound was pillaged, and the possessions of the Oba and his court became spoils of war. The expedition destroyed the city and its culture, and it marked the decline of Benin art.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: The fabrics enjoyed a strong reception in West Africa starting in the 1880s, when Dutch and Scottish trading vessels introduced them in West African ports. Initial demand may have been driven by a taste for batik among the Belanda Hitam. They were West Africans recruited between 1831 and 1872 from the Dutch Gold Coast to serve in the Dutch colonial army in Indonesia.

During the French colonial occupation of the Sahel, French engineers and architects helped popularize a "Neo-Sudanese" style. It was based on local traditional architecture but emphasized symmetry and monumentality. The rebuilt Great Mosque of Djenné served as a model for the new style.

A 19th-century Benin ivory leopard carving in the British Museum is stylized, with spots of inlaid copper. Each of its main body parts was made from a different tusk. Leopards were often shown in pairs in the Oba's palace in Benin City, as an expression of superiority.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: The term "Ankara" comes from the Hausa name for Accra, which served as a hub for African prints in the 19th century. It was first used by Nigerian Hausa tradesmen. The Igbo people of Nigeria call the cloth "Abada".

The 19th-century Great Mosque of Zaria, in present-day Nigeria, is an exceptional example of the eastern Hausa style of earthen architecture. It has parabolic arches and a roof of shallow domes. The Hausa style is generally plainer on the outside but has diverse interior decoration and much greater use of wood.

When British forces pillaged Oba Ovonramwen's compound in 1897, the objects were rounded up with little regard for their meaning. No systematic record was kept of their grouping or placement. Many were sold in London to defray the cost of the expedition, and most of the pieces of Benin art were auctioned off there.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: Many members of the Belanda Hitam retired to Elmina, in modern Ghana. There they may have provided an early market for Dutch imitation batik cloth.

When British troops took possession of the palace in 1897, they reported 18 altars dedicated to previous Obas. Before the British conquest, an Oba's courtyard was the focal point for rituals in his honor. A newly installed Oba kept his father's altar active with regular sacrifices of food or animal blood, and did the same for his mother if she held the title of Iyoba, or queen mother.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

war.text: In 1867 the Mandinka capital of Kansala, in the Kaabu federation, came under siege from an army led by Alfa Omar of Labé and Alfa Molo Balde. At the climax of the eleven-day Battle of Kansala, Mansaba Janke Waali Sanneh (also called Mansaba Dianke Walli) ordered the city's gunpowder stores set afire. The explosion killed the Mandinka defenders and 75% of the attackers, and Kansala was obliterated, ending Mandinka hegemony in the region.

For most of the 19th century the Ashante Empire remained a powerful force in West Africa. Britain fought repeated Anglo-Ashanti wars in the Gold Coast in 1823, 1824–1831, 1863–64, 1873–74, 1895–96 and 1900, and only the last two were clear British victories. The British Empire annexed the Ashante Empire in 1900 following four Anglo-Ashanti wars.

Formed in 1808 after the British Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act 1807, the West Africa Squadron of the Royal Navy patrolled the coast of West Africa to suppress the Atlantic slave trade. It captured about 6% of the transatlantic slave ships and freed about 150,000 Africans. Sailors considered it one of the worst postings because of extremely high levels of tropical disease, and between 1830 and 1865 almost 1,600 of them died on duty with the Squadron, principally of disease.

Kansala was the imperial capital of Kaabu, a federation of Mandinka kingdoms in the Senegambia region. It was captured by Fula forces from the Futa Jallon during the 19th century Fula jihads, after a siege that ended in the city being obliterated by an explosion that killed the defenders and 75% of the attackers. Kansala remained under Fula control until the Portuguese suppression of the kingdom around the turn of the 20th century.

Osei Bonsu ruled the Ashante Empire from 1807 to 1824 and continued its territorial consolidation and expansion. At its height, the empire included most of present-day Ghana and large parts of Côte d'Ivoire.

The military culture of the Mali Empire's Mandinka people influenced many later states in West Africa. Institutions from the empire also survived in the 19th century army of Samory Ture, who saw himself as the heir to Old Mali's legacy.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: After the Battle of Kansala, in which an explosion of the city's gunpowder killed the defenders and 75% of the attackers, the surviving attackers lacked the manpower to pursue their aim of conquering the whole Kaabu empire. Instead, the area called Fuladu, in southern Senegal, gained its independence. Alfa Molo Balde became its first king.

Kaabu's successor states across Senegambia continued to thrive even after Kansala fell. This lasted until the remaining kingdoms were fully incorporated into the British, Portuguese and French spheres of influence during the Scramble for Africa.

French West Africa was created in 1895 as a union of Senegal, French Sudan, French Guinea and Ivory Coast, later growing into a federation of eight territories. In 1904, both Mauritania and Niger were classed as Military Territories, ruled by the federation in conjunction with officers of the French Colonial Forces.

Up until the 1860s, Kaabu had successfully repulsed various Fula armies on numerous occasions at the fort of Berekolong. Only in 1867 did the capital at Kansala come under a siege that ended in its destruction, when the Mansaba had the city's gunpowder stores set afire, killing the Mandinka defenders and 75% of the attackers.

Joint operations between the US Navy and the West Africa Squadron began in 1820 with the dispatch of the USS Cyane to the West African coast. Ironically, the United States had captured the Cyane from the Royal Navy in February 1815, in a 40-minute engagement in the middle of the night off Portugal.

literature.text: West African manuscripts from the late 19th and early 20th centuries survive in northern Ghana, Mali, Nigeria, and Senegal. They cover Arabic grammar, astronomy, history, law, medicine and healing, numerology, poetry, Sufism, and theology. Many are chronicles, letters, and lists such as kings lists and imam lists.

Writing in West Africa was not only in Arabic. Manuscripts from northern Ghana, Mali, Nigeria, and Senegal include Fulfulde, Hausa, and Wolof Ajami market editions, meaning local languages written in Arabic-based script. One surviving example is a copy of the Book of Genesis composed in Fulfulde Ajami.

Manuscripts from Ségou, Mali, record a jihad in West Africa. It was led by Al-Hāj Umar Taal, who lived from 1797 to 1864 and was the leader of the Fuuta Tooro Tijāniyya. These writings show how the wars of the century were also documented by West African authors themselves.

Nigeria holds many handwritten copies of the Quran among its manuscripts. Some of these have been dated to the early 19th century. They are part of the large body of West African manuscripts written in the Arabic script.

The al-Imam Essayouti library in Timbuktu holds texts of which the majority were written between the 18th and 20th centuries. Its oldest text dates from 1615. This means its collection spans from well before to well after the Industrial era.

The phrase "mosque-university of Sankore" was first coined in 1897 by the French author and explorer Felix Dubois. Kwame Nkrumah later popularised it as the "University of Sankore" in 1961. Yet there is no evidence that Timbuktu ever had an organised institution equivalent to a university.

Many African groups had encountered the Latin and Arabic scripts for centuries but rarely adopted them widely until the 19th century, because they did not find them necessary for their own societies. Ajamiyya writing, an Arabic-derived script, was a notable exception.

science.text: Commercial gold mining began in what is today Ghana in the early 19th century, with Europeans later establishing several mines during the colonial period. By 1900, Ghana, then known as the Gold Coast, had become a major supplier of gold in the British Empire.

Sailors in the Royal Navy considered the West Africa Squadron one of the worst postings because of the extremely high levels of tropical disease to which its members were exposed. Between 1830 and 1865, almost 1,600 sailors died during duty with the Squadron, principally of disease. Crews were exhausted by heavy rowing under extreme tropical conditions and exposed to fevers with after-effects from which they seldom recovered, and their sickness and death rates were significantly higher than in the rest of the Royal Navy.

The first documented large-scale mining operation in Ghana was at Obuasi, where gold was discovered in 1897. The Ashanti Goldfields Corporation was established that year, marking the start of large-scale industrial gold mining. Local artisanal mining, known as galamsey, had come before.

Obuasi has produced more than 35 million ounces of gold since its discovery in the late 19th century. The Ashanti Region has played a central role in gold mining in Ghana, dating back to the 19th century. Today it is home to AngloGold Ashanti at Obuasi.

politics.text: French West Africa began in 1895 as a union of Senegal, French Sudan, French Guinea and Ivory Coast. It was placed on a permanent footing in 1904. In theory its Governors-General reported directly to the Minister of Colonies in Paris, while individual colonies reported only to Dakar.

The Berlin Conference met from November 1884 to February 1885. It did not name Togo or Kamerun, but it confirmed the steps the Powers had to follow to recognise each other's territorial claims in West Africa. Germany's claims were effectively recognised because Gustav Nachtigal had followed those steps.

The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron was formed in 1808, after Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act 1807, to suppress the Atlantic slave trade. Over its operations it captured about 6% of transatlantic slave ships and freed about 150,000 Africans. Many freed people from inland regions were left to find their own way home, often got lost and endured appalling conditions, and it is estimated that up to a quarter of those who could not stay in Freetown or easily return home died before being fully released from the legal and practical entanglements of their past. Historians still debate how much the Squadron really achieved.

Usman dan Fodio's jihadist war created an empire including parts of northern Nigeria, Benin, and Cameroon, with Sokoto as its capital. He then retired to teach and write, handing the empire to his son Muhammed Bello. The Sokoto Caliphate lasted until 1903, when the British conquered northern Nigeria.

On 5 July 1884, Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty with Mlapa III, ruler of Togo, a village known today as Togoville. It set up a German protectorate over a stretch of coast. This became the basis of the future German colony of Togoland.

In 1914, Blaise Diagne became the first African elected to represent Senegal in the French Parliament. The Four Communes of Senegal had been entitled to elect a deputy in several periods, including 1879 to 1940. The Four Communes were Dakar, Gorée, Saint-Louis and Rufisque.

Slavery was formally illegal in all French land from 1848, but that law applied only to French citizens, so indigenous subjects without citizenship were not obliged to obey it and slave owners in French West Africa kept their slaves. From 1903 to 1905, under pressure from French abolitionists, French authorities began enforcing anti-slavery laws against indigenous slave owners: the laws against the slave trade were enforced, and fugitive slaves were no longer returned to their owners. In 1905 slavery was officially abolished in most of the territory. From 1906 to 1911, over a million slaves fled from their masters to their earlier homes.

After Awole committed ritual suicide, Oyo's central authority collapsed into a scramble for the throne, with an interregnum of almost twenty years. In 1817 Afonja seceded Ilorin from Oyo with the help of Oyo Muslims. In 1823, Afonja was killed by his erstwhile allies Shehu Alimi and Solagberu, who was himself later killed by Alimi's son, and Ilorin became part of the Sokoto Caliphate.

In 1884 the syndicate for West Africa was founded with Bismarck's support to take over the internal administration of the West African colonies. The companies involved refused to do this alone and demanded a German government administration instead. Bismarck's idea of indirect rule failed, and the syndicate dissolved in 1886.

On 20 February 1888, Louis Gustave Binger entered Kong and made agreements with its leaders as part of French efforts to control the region. This made Kong a target for Samory Touré. In 1895 the French column under Col. Monteil sparked a popular resistance movement as it passed. Monteil fought a battle with Wassoulonke forces on the 14th, and the French were forced to retreat and abandon Kong, which pledged fealty to Samory in April.

The Kong Empire's ruling aristocracy derived no legitimacy from Islam and did not implement Sharia. This made Kong fundamentally different from the jihad states of West Africa. Kong was nonetheless an important centre of Islamic study and trade.

The United States sent ships to help the British blockade of the slave trade, beginning in 1820 with the USS Cyane. The US contingent, known as the Africa Squadron, grew and strengthened considerably after the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842. The cooperation drew bitter protest from southern planters in the United States.

When Captain Hugh Clapperton visited Oyo-Ile in 1825, under Alaafin Majotu, the empire was already in decline. His party recorded passing numerous Oyo villages burned by the Fulani of Ilorin. Ilorin then besieged Offa and began raiding, burning and pillaging villages in Oyo, eventually destroying the capital Oyo-Ile in 1835. Clapperton also noticed a shortage of horses, which might be explained by most of the empire's soldiers and cavalry being stationed at Ilorin under Afonja and later Alimi's successors.

philosophy.text: In 1804, Usman dan Fodio launched the Fulani War as a jihad, a war of religious conquest, among a population restless about high taxes and discontented with its leaders. He had accused the Hausa leadership of practising an impure version of Islam and of moral corruption. Jihad fever swept northern Nigeria, with strong support among both the Fulani and the Hausa.

Before the 20th century, African philosophy was mainly conducted and passed on orally, by philosophers whose names have been lost to history. It included folklore, wise sayings and religious ideas, as well as philosophical concepts such as Ubuntu, often summarized as "I am because we are."

Vodún teaches a supreme creator divinity, under whom are lesser spirits called vodúns. Practised by the Aja, Ewe, and Fon peoples, it has no central authority and much diversity among its followers. Its most prominent form of divination is Fá, governed by a society of initiates.
Nana Asma'u (1793-1864) was a princess of the Sokoto Caliphate, in present-day Nigeria. She is named as one of the leading women philosophers and writers of the caliphate.

Adinkra is a set of symbols developed by the Akan to represent concepts and aphorisms. Oral tradition attributes its origin to Gyaman in modern-day Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire. Kwame Anthony Appiah says the symbols helped support the transmission of a complex and nuanced body of practice and belief.

Vodún faced attempted suppression during the Christianisation projects of the 19th century. In 1890, France invaded Dahomey and dethroned its king, Béhanzin. In 1900 the French abolished the Kingdom of Dahomey.
Among the Fon, a common belief is that the head is the seat of a person's soul. The head is therefore of symbolic importance in Vodún.

Some Mandé-speaking groups, such as the Bambara, converted to Islam as late as the 19th century, with some retaining their traditional beliefs. Muslim Mandinka also hold beliefs such as the rituals of initiation groups like Chiwara and Dwo, and faith in the power of nyama, a spiritual power existing in nature.

Under British rule, local elites developed in West Africa with new values and philosophies, which changed the overall cultural development. The colonial school curriculum played a role in this. Indigenous cultures and interests were ignored, and autonomous educational systems were the first step to modernising indigenous culture.

culture.text: In 1824, the Paris-based Société de Géographie offered a 9,000 franc prize to the first non-Muslim to reach Timbuktu and return with information about it. The Scotsman Gordon Laing arrived in August 1826, but the following month he was killed by local Muslims who were fearful of European intervention. Laing never returned to claim the prize.

Vodún is a traditional religion practiced by the Aja, Ewe, and Fon peoples of Benin, Togo, Ghana, and Nigeria. Its followers honour lesser spirits called vodúns, believed to physically manifest in shrines. The spirits are given offerings, typically including animal sacrifice: the animal's throat is cut and the shrine is covered in its blood, to feed the spirit's acɛ. The article also says there is ample evidence that human sacrifice was performed in parts of West Africa before European colonisation, such as in the Dahomey kingdom during the Annual Customs of Dahomey.

The Frenchman René Caillié reached Timbuktu in 1828, travelling alone and disguised as a Muslim. Unlike Gordon Laing, he was able to return safely and claim the prize offered by the Société de Géographie.

Under British West Africa, the first step in modernising indigenous culture was the creation of autonomous educational systems. A new social order and European influences in schools and libraries helped mould the region's culture, and local elites developed with new values and philosophies.

In Sierra Leone in the 19th century about half of the population consisted of enslaved people. Among the Vai people, three quarters were slaves, while among the Ashanti and Yoruba a third of the population was enslaved.

Vodún has several all-male secret societies, including Oró and Egúngún, into which individuals receive initiation. The most prominent form of divination is Fá, itself governed by a society of initiates.

Attempted suppression of Vodún came with the Christianisation projects of the 19th century. Earlier, vodúnsɛntó were among the enslaved Africans transported to the Americas during the Atlantic slave trade of the 16th to the 19th century. There their traditional religions influenced new religions such as Haitian Vodou, Louisiana Voodoo, and Brazilian Candomblé Jejé. Ouidah was a major slave embarkation point from the 1670s through to the 1860s.

Following conquest and abolition by the French, over a million slaves in French West Africa fled from their masters to earlier homes between 1906 and 1911. The Sokoto Caliphate abolished slavery in 1900.

The American sailor Robert Adams claimed to have visited Timbuktu in 1812 while enslaved in Northern Africa. His story quickly became controversial, and more recent scholarship concludes that discrepancies in his description make it unlikely he ever visited the city.
